summary: Antigua and Barbuda waives visas for well over 100 nationalities — including the US, Canada, the UK, the EU and most Commonwealth countries, normally for stays of up to six months — while CARICOM nationals move freely and everyone else applies to a High Commission or embassy before travelling.

fee.notes: Approximate for a single-entry visitor visa — multiple-entry visas cost more; confirm the current fee with the mission handling your application.
Approximate — extension fees are set by the Immigration Department and are payable in East Caribbean dollars; confirm the current amount in St John's.
Single applicant; higher fees apply for couples and families. Applicants must show remote income and valid health insurance.

passportValidity.text: Your passport must be valid for the whole of your intended stay. Airlines and some officials still apply a six-month rule, so travel with at least six months' validity where you can.

vaccinations.name: Yellow fever
vaccinations.text: A yellow fever vaccination certificate is required from travellers aged one year and over arriving from — or having recently transited — a country with risk of yellow fever transmission. No vaccination is required if you fly in directly from Europe, North America or the rest of the Caribbean.

travelInsurance.text: Travel insurance is not checked at the border for ordinary visits, but medical care is private and paid for up front — travel with cover that includes medical evacuation, which is the expensive part on a small island.

onwardTicket.text: Visitors must hold a return or onward ticket; immigration officers also ask for the address where you are staying and set the length of stay accordingly.

proofOfFunds.text: No fixed amount is published. Officers may ask how you will support yourself, particularly if you request a long stay or have no confirmed accommodation.

declarations.name: Immigration and customs declaration
declarations.text: Every arriving passenger completes an immigration and customs declaration. Antigua and Barbuda has been moving this online — complete the electronic form if your airline or the Immigration Department directs you to one, otherwise fill in the card handed out on the flight.

currencyLimits.text: Cash or bearer instruments worth XCD 10,000 or more (roughly USD 3,700) must be declared on arrival and departure.

notes: Firearms and ammunition are strictly controlled — bringing any into the country without a permit leads to arrest, including for cruise and yacht passengers.
Fresh produce, plants, meat and dairy are restricted to protect local agriculture; declare anything you are carrying.
Drones must be declared and may require permission from the authorities before use.

payments.text: Hotels, restaurants and larger shops take cards, and US dollars are accepted almost everywhere at a rate near EC$2.60 (banks give EC$2.70). Carry small East Caribbean notes for buses, beach bars and market stalls.

safety.text: Antigua and Barbuda is a calm destination for visitors; the usual issues are opportunistic theft from beaches and rental cars, and strong currents on the Atlantic coast. Hurricane season runs from June to November.

source.name: U.S. Department of State — Antigua and Barbuda Travel Advisory

bestTimeToVisit.text: December to April is dry, breezy and reliably sunny. May to November is hotter and wetter, with the hurricane peak from August to October — but far cheaper.

tips.text: You cannot drive on your home licence alone — car hire companies issue a temporary Antiguan driving permit (around EC$50) on the spot when you show a valid licence. Driving is on the left.
The hurricane season runs from June to November, peaking in August and September. Book flexible fares and take travel insurance that covers weather disruption if you travel then.
Barbuda is a separate island — reached by a short flight or the ferry from St John's, both weather-dependent. Do not plan a same-day return connection to an international flight.
US dollars are accepted island-wide, but change is usually given in East Caribbean dollars — check which currency a quoted price is in before you pay.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Antigua and Barbuda?
faq.answer: Probably not. Antigua and Barbuda waives visas for more than 100 nationalities, including the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, the EU and most Commonwealth countries — visitors are normally admitted for up to six months. CARICOM nationals move freely. Everyone else applies for a visitor visa at an Antigua and Barbuda High Commission, embassy or consulate before travelling.

faq.question: How long can I stay in Antigua and Barbuda without a visa?
faq.answer: Immigration officers grant the length of stay they think your trip needs, up to six months for most visa-free visitors. Ask for what you actually need at the desk — extending later means a trip to the Immigration Department in St John's and a fee.

faq.question: How much passport validity do I need?
faq.answer: Officially your passport must be valid for the duration of your stay. Airlines frequently apply their own six-month rule, so renew if you have less than six months left.

faq.question: Do I need a return ticket?
faq.answer: Yes. Visitors are expected to hold a confirmed onward or return ticket and to give an address in Antigua or Barbuda. Both are commonly checked at the immigration desk.

faq.question: Can I work remotely from Antigua and Barbuda?
faq.answer: Yes — the Nomad Digital Residence lets remote workers and their families live in Antigua and Barbuda for up to two years. It costs around USD 1,500 for a single applicant and requires proof of remote income and health insurance. Short visa-free visits do not permit local employment.
